sections.abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title> <jats:p>Central sleep apnea (CSA) is a rare form of sleep disordered breathing with repeated apneic episodes with absence of associated respiratory effort. CSA due to medication is well described in literature with opiate therapy. Baclofen which is a gamma-aminobutyric acid-B agonist with muscle relaxant properties has been implicated in CSA. We present a rare case of CSA likely due to chronic baclofen use. Patient underwent a polysomnogram (PSG) while on baclofen therapy which revealed severe central sleep apnea. Patient was weaned off baclofen therapy completely and a subsequent PSG was performed which revealed resolution of the CSA.</jats:p> </jats:sec> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Methods</jats:title> <jats:p>28 year old male with cerebral palsy and neurogenic bladder who presented for evaluation of snoring, chronic insomnia and non-refreshing sleep.</jats:p> <jats:p>Overnight PSG was performed for further evaluation of his sleep related complaints while on chronic baclofen therapy, which revealed severe central sleep apnea. Trial of positive airway pressure therapy for treatment of CSA and supplemental oxygen therapy were attempted during the PSG but had to be terminated due to intolerance.</jats:p> <jats:p>Echocardiography and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain were performed to rule out congestive heart failure and Chiari malformation respectively, which revealed no underlying pathology to explaining the CSA. CSA in this patient was thought to be associated with chronic baclofen therapy. Patient was weaned off baclofen with repeat PSG revealing resolution of the CSA.</jats:p> </jats:sec> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Results</jats:title> <jats:p>1st diagnostic PSG - on Baclofen:</jats:p> <jats:p>139 central apneas, 6 obstructive apneas, 3 mixed apnea, and 38 hypopneas.</jats:p> <jats:p>This study showed severe central sleep apnea.</jats:p> <jats:p>The apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) was 51.5, REM index 21.8 and supine index 51.5.</jats:p> <jats:p>Central apnea index 39.5.</jats:p> <jats:p>Respiratory events were associated with moderate oxygen desaturations.</jats:p> <jats:p>The mean oxygen saturation during the study was 92.8%, with a minimum oxygen saturation of 81%.</jats:p> <jats:p>The patient spent 2.9 minutes with an oxygen saturation equal to or less than 88% for the entire study.</jats:p> <jats:p>CPAP titration was attempted and aborted, due to patient having difficulty tolerating CPAP.</jats:p> <jats:p>Supplemental oxygen was briefly added at 0.5 LPM, which was also discontinued due to patient complaining of burning sensation in the nose.</jats:p> <jats:p>Head of the bed was elevated at several levels (20 degrees, 30 degrees and 45 degrees) which did not attenuate the respiratory events.</jats:p> <jats:p>2nd Diagnostic PSG – patient weaned off baclofen for study –</jats:p> <jats:p>Sleep efficiency reduced at 59.4%.</jats:p> <jats:p>Sleep onset latency 7.5 minutes.</jats:p> <jats:p>REM latency 163 minutes.</jats:p> <jats:p>100% of total sleep time in supine position</jats:p> <jats:p>Moderate snoring.</jats:p> <jats:p>The apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) was 4.2, REM index 36.5 and supine index 4.2.</jats:p> <jats:p>Respiratory events were mainly noted using REM sleep.</jats:p> <jats:p>Respiratory events were associated with moderate oxygen desaturations.</jats:p> <jats:p>The mean oxygen saturation during the study was 93.9%, with a minimum oxygen saturation of 83%.</jats:p> <jats:p>The patient spent 1.2 minutes with an oxygen saturation equal to or less than 88% for the entire study.</jats:p> <jats:p>Labs and imaging –</jats:p> <jats:p>Workup for severe central sleep apnea after first diagnostic sleep study –</jats:p> <jats:p>Echo and MRI brain, which revealed no underlying pathology explaining his central sleep apnea.
